name: Lockora Security Audit – Security Scanner, Hardening & Integrity
author: Guido Schad

sections.description:
Lockora Security Audit is a lightweight WordPress security audit, security scanner, and hardening plugin built for site owners, agencies, and security-conscious developers. Run a full security check from Tools > Lockora Security Audit (or via WP-CLI) and get a weighted security score out of 100, concrete evidence for every finding, and reversible hardening controls.

100% free and local-first: Core file integrity verification, wp-content anomaly scanning, hidden-administrator auditing, web-root exposure probes, scheduled scans, email/webhook alerts, Site Health integration, and WP-CLI CI support all ship in the free plugin with no Pro paywall, no external account, and no telemetry.

Built and maintained by WP Server Guard, WordPress server security and hardening specialists.

WordPress Security Scanner & Core File Integrity

  • Weighted security score & scan history. Score your site’s security posture out of 100 and compare current findings against previous scans to spot regressions fast.
  • WordPress core file integrity check. Verify core files against official WordPress.org checksums to detect altered, missing, or unexpected files, with CSV and TXT exports.
  • wp-content anomaly scanner. Bounded scanning for executable uploads, unexpected PHP files outside standard code directories, runtime executables, and exposed backup or secret-like files — with CSV/TXT exports and one-click clipboard copy.
  • Must-use plugin & drop-in inventory. Hashes mu-plugins and drop-in files and flags entries added or changed since the previous scan.
  • Web-root exposure & public security checks. Detects reachable .git, .env, database dumps, backup copies, archives, debug.log, readme.html, uploads directory listing, PHP execution inside uploads, and author archive user enumeration — using loopback probes that distinguish real file downloads from “200 OK” error pages.

Hidden Administrator & Privileged Account Audit

  • Hidden admin & privilege escalation detection. Compares raw user capability records against WordPress’s standard Administrator query to uncover hidden Administrators, direct capability grants, privileged custom roles, runtime-granted privileges, malformed capability metadata, and multisite super administrators.
  • Administrator posture checks. Flags default usernames, excess or inactive administrators, user ID 1 exposure, administrator application passwords, and provides an exportable admin username/email inventory.

One-Click Hardening, Salt Rotation & Security Headers

  • Reversible hardening toggles. Toggle XML-RPC, public REST user routes, generator tag output, and basic HTTP security headers on or off safely from one screen.
  • Authentication keys & salt rotation. Audits WordPress authentication keys and salts with explicit, guarded actions to generate missing salts or rotate existing keys stored in wp-config.php.
  • Transport, runtime & update posture. Checks HTTPS, HTTP security headers, SSL certificate expiry, database table prefix, automatic update readiness, login protection / 2FA plugin presence, PHP version support via WordPress.org Serve Happy data, and core/plugin/theme update status.

Scheduled Security Scans, Alerts, WP-CLI & Agency Reporting

  • Scheduled scans & diff-only alerts. Run automated scans twice daily, daily, or weekly through WP-Cron. Email and Slack-compatible webhook alerts fire only when findings are new or worse than the previous scan.
  • WordPress Site Health integration. Surfaces your Lockora security summary and key configuration checks directly under Tools > Site Health > Status.
  • WP-CLI & CI/CD pipeline support. Run wp lockora scan and wp lockora report with --format=json, --format=csv, and --strict for automated deployment gates and agency monitoring.
  • Optional vulnerability scanner (Wordfence Intelligence). Configure your own Wordfence Intelligence API key to match known vulnerabilities locally against installed WordPress core, plugin, and theme versions.
  • Optional AI client reports (WordPress 7.0+). Generate sanitized, client-ready security audit reports using your site’s configured WordPress AI Connector, with customizable agency footer attribution.
  • Developer hook for integrations. Fires lockora_scan_completed with scan scores and finding counts so monitoring or activity-log tools can record every audit.

Environment-Aware Scanning (Local, Dev, Staging & Production)

On local and development copies served from a local host name, server-specific checks (HTTPS, security headers, debug output, and web-root files) are automatically relaxed to warnings while core integrity, vulnerabilities, accounts, and file anomalies stay strict. Public sites declaring a non-production environment are flagged and keep full production checks.

Works Well With Who Changed It?

Lockora finds security weaknesses and misconfigurations. Who Changed It? – User Activity Log, Audit Log & Change Tracker shows what changed, who changed it, and when — with tamper-evident hash chaining, severity classification, inline field diffs, and alerts. Use both together to connect every security finding directly to the user action that caused it.

External Services

Lockora Security Audit may connect to external services only when a scan runs (started by an administrator, by WP-CLI, or by a scheduled scan the administrator enabled), when an alert is sent, or when an administrator generates an AI client report.

During a scan the plugin also sends HTTP requests to the site’s own public URL (loopback requests) to inspect response headers, debug.log and readme.html reachability, uploads directory behavior, author archive redirects, and whether files such as /.git/HEAD, /.env, or backups in the web root can be downloaded, and it opens a TLS connection to the site’s own hostname to read the SSL certificate expiry date. These requests stay within the site being scanned and send no data to third parties.

WordPress.org APIs:
* Used for WordPress core checksums, PHP version support status, and WordPress core/plugin/theme update data. When WordPress’s cached update data is missing or older than its normal refresh interval, a scan asks WordPress to refresh it using the core update functions.
* Data sent: the site’s WordPress version and locale for core checksums and PHP compatibility; WordPress itself may send installed plugin and theme slugs/versions to WordPress.org when update data is refreshed.
* WordPress.org terms: https://wordpress.org/about/terms/
* WordPress.org privacy policy: https://wordpress.org/about/privacy/

Wordfence Intelligence:
* Optional.
* Used only when a Wordfence Intelligence API key is configured and an administrator runs a scan that includes vulnerability matching.
* Used to retrieve vulnerability data and match it locally against installed WordPress core, plugin, and theme versions.
* Data sent: the configured Wordfence Intelligence API key is sent in an Authorization header when requesting the vulnerability feed. Installed software details are not sent by this plugin to the Wordfence Intelligence endpoint; matching is performed locally after the feed is retrieved.
* Wordfence Intelligence terms: https://www.wordfence.com/wordfence-intelligence-terms-and-conditions/
* Wordfence privacy policy: https://www.wordfence.com/privacy-policy/

Alert webhook:
* Optional.
* Used only when an administrator saves a webhook URL under Scheduled Scans and Alerts, when a scheduled scan finds new or worsened findings, or when the administrator sends a test alert.
* Data sent: site URL and name, scan time, environment type, score and counts, and the ID, status, severity, title, and recommendation of each new or worsened finding. Evidence (which can contain account names, email addresses, or file paths) is not sent.
* The service that receives the webhook is chosen by the administrator. Review that service’s terms and privacy policy before saving a webhook URL.

Alert emails are sent through WordPress’s own wp_mail() to the recipients the administrator configures, and include the evidence of each new or worsened finding.

WordPress AI Client / Connectors:
* Optional.
* Used only when the administrator clicks Generate Client Report.
* Data sent: sanitized scan findings, score, counts, and recommendations needed to generate a client-facing report. The plugin is designed not to send passwords, salts, API keys, raw logs, full user lists, or file contents.
* The configured AI provider is controlled by the site owner’s WordPress Connector settings.
* Terms and privacy policy: these depend on the AI provider configured by the site owner in WordPress. Site owners should review the selected provider’s terms and privacy policy before enabling AI reports.
sections.installation:
1. Upload the lockora-security-audit folder to /wp-content/plugins/.
  2. Activate Lockora Security Audit from the Plugins screen.
  3. Go to Tools > Lockora Security Audit.
  4. Click Run Scan.
sections.faq:
Is Lockora Security Audit completely free?

Yes. Core file integrity checks, wp-content anomaly scanning, hidden administrator auditing, web-root exposure probes, reversible hardening toggles, salt rotation, scheduled WP-Cron scans, email and Slack-compatible webhook alerts, Site Health integration, and WP-CLI commands all ship in the free plugin with no Pro paywall or external account required.

Does Lockora Security Audit replace a firewall like Wordfence?

No — they complement each other. A web application firewall (WAF) blocks malicious HTTP requests in real time, whereas Lockora audits your WordPress security posture, verifies core and MU-plugin file integrity, detects exposed files (.env, .git, debug.log, backups), uncovers hidden administrator accounts, and monitors configuration regressions over time. Many sites run Lockora alongside a firewall and an activity log such as Who Changed It?.

Does Lockora check for exposed .env, .git, or backup files?

Yes. Lockora checks the web root and wp-content for sensitive files including .git, .env, SQL database dumps, backup archives, debug.log, and readme.html. For web-root exposures, it confirms reachability with loopback HTTP requests that distinguish an actual downloadable file from a soft “200 OK” HTML error page.

How do I run WordPress security audits from WP-CLI or CI pipelines?

Use wp lockora scan to run a fresh audit and wp lockora report to print the latest results. Both commands support --format=json and --format=csv (progress messages go to stderr so stdout stays machine-parseable) plus a --strict flag that exits non-zero when failures are present, making it straightforward to gate deployments in CI/CD.

Does Lockora Security Audit fix every issue automatically?

No. It provides reversible hardening toggles for selected low-risk settings. Other findings should be reviewed by an administrator, developer, or host.

How do scheduled scans and alerts work?

Under Tools > Lockora Security Audit > Scheduled Scans and Alerts, choose a frequency and an alert level. Scheduled scans run through WP-Cron. After each scheduled scan Lockora compares the results with the previous scan and sends an alert only for findings that are new or got worse (for example warning to failure), plus inventory findings that list newly added must-use plugins, drop-ins, or privileged accounts. Nothing is sent when nothing got worse. The first scheduled scan with no earlier scan on record lists every open finding at the alert level as a baseline.

Alerts go to the recipients you enter (or the site admin email) and, optionally, to an https webhook. Use Send Test Alert to confirm delivery. If DISABLE_WP_CRON is set, a server cron job must call wp-cron.php for scheduled scans to run. On multisite, scheduled scans are configured on the main site because they cover the whole network. Webhooks are sent with wp_safe_remote_post(), which refuses private network addresses.

Developers can use the lockora_send_scan_alert and lockora_alert_webhook_payload filters and the lockora_scan_alert_sent action.

What changes on local and development sites?

Lockora reads wp_get_environment_type(). When the site declares a local or development environment and is served from a local host name (localhost, private IP addresses, or names ending in .local, .test, .localhost, .ddev.site, and similar), checks that describe the developer machine rather than the site, such as HTTPS, security headers, debug output, and .git or .env files in the web root, are relaxed: failures become low-severity warnings and the evidence notes the production status. Core integrity, vulnerabilities, accounts, and file anomalies are never relaxed.

If a site declares a local or development environment but is served from a public host name, Lockora keeps all checks and reports the mismatch. Staging sites are scanned with production rules. Developers can change the relaxed checks with the lockora_environment_relaxed_checks filter and the local host name detection with lockora_is_local_hostname.

Who can use Lockora on multisite?

On multisite, only network administrators (the manage_network_options capability) can open Lockora, run scans, and export results, because scans read network-wide data and some actions change wp-config.php for every site. Developers can change the required capability with the lockora_required_capability filter; changes to wp-config.php always require network administrator rights on multisite.

Does Lockora Security Audit require AI?

No. The scanner works without AI on WordPress 6.0 and newer. AI client reports are optional and require WordPress 7.0 or newer with AI Client support plus a configured AI Connector.

Does Lockora Security Audit include a vulnerability database?

No. It can optionally use a configured Wordfence Intelligence API key for known vulnerability matching.

Does the wp-content scan validate every plugin and theme file?

No. Plugin, theme, must-use plugin, and language directories contain legitimate executable files and are excluded from this anomaly pass by default. Lockora checks their update and vulnerability posture separately. The anomaly scan focuses on uploads, the wp-content root, cache and upgrade locations, backups, and secret-like files.

Developers can tune the scan with the lockora_wp_content_allowed_files, lockora_wp_content_excluded_paths, lockora_wp_content_executable_extensions, lockora_wp_content_sensitive_extensions, lockora_wp_content_archive_extensions, lockora_wp_content_scan_max_files, and lockora_wp_content_max_reported_paths filters. Allowed and excluded paths are relative to the wp-content directory.

Can Lockora detect hidden WordPress administrators?

Lockora compares raw user capability records with WordPress’s normal Administrator query and lists every account it finds with elevated authority. It flags standard Administrators omitted from the normal query, direct capability grants, privileged custom roles, privileges added by runtime capability filters, duplicate or malformed capability metadata, newly privileged accounts, and multisite super administrators.

Every role and capability record is checked directly in the database, however many users the site has; ordinary single-role subscribers and customers are excluded in SQL. Privileges added by runtime capability filters need each account loaded through WordPress, so that pass checks the newest accounts first, up to the lockora_privileged_account_scan_max_users limit (2,000 by default).

The audit does not read password hashes, application passwords, or authentication keys. It reports only whether an unexpired WordPress session exists and never exports session tokens. The separate application password check counts application passwords on administrator accounts and reads only their last-used date. Code-only authentication backdoors that do not grant capabilities to a WordPress account require separate source inspection. Developers can tune the privileged capability list and workload limits with the lockora_privileged_capabilities, lockora_privileged_account_scan_max_users, and lockora_privileged_account_max_reported_accounts filters.

Does Lockora Security Audit send secrets to AI providers?

The plugin is designed to send sanitized scan findings only. It does not intentionally send passwords, salts, API keys, raw logs, user lists, or file contents.
sections.changelog:
0.6.0

  • Added scheduled scans (twice daily, daily, weekly) with email and webhook alerts for findings that are new or worse than the previous scan, plus a test alert button.
  • Added environment awareness: server-specific checks are relaxed on local and development copies served from a local host name, and public sites that declare a non-production environment are flagged.
  • Added a web-root exposure check for .git, .env, database dumps, backup copies, archives, and logs, with loopback probes that distinguish real downloads from error pages.
  • Added a must-use plugin and drop-in inventory that flags entries added or changed since the previous scan. It replaces the mu-plugins directory check, which reported a missing directory as a failure.
  • Security: on multisite, Lockora now requires network administrator rights. Sub-site administrators could previously rotate wp-config.php salts for the whole network and export the super administrator list.
  • Fixed: the debug display check failed on almost every production site, because WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY defaults to true even though it only applies while WP_DEBUG is on. It now checks WP_DEBUG together with WP_DEBUG_DISPLAY and the server’s display_errors setting.
  • Fixed: the privileged account audit only examined the oldest 2,000 users, so on large sites the newest (most likely malicious) accounts were never checked. Role and capability records are now checked for every account, and runtime grants are checked newest first.
  • Fixed: an unreadable directory inside wp-admin or wp-includes crashed the core integrity scan.
  • Fixed: normal site-root files such as robots.txt, ads.txt, and verification files, and a deleted readme.html, failed the core integrity check. Executable files in the site root are now a warning; executable extras inside wp-admin and wp-includes still fail.
  • Fixed: the privileged account CSV export wrote a PHP 8.4 deprecation notice into the downloaded file.
  • Fixed: wp lockora scan --format=json and --format=csv printed progress and score lines to standard output, breaking JSON and CSV parsing in CI. Progress now goes to standard error.
  • Fixed: opening the Lockora page after an update ran a full scan inside the page request, which could exceed the PHP time limit. The scan now runs in the background while the previous results are shown.
  • Fixed: missing or stale WordPress update data was reported as “no updates available”. Scans now refresh stale update data and report when it is unavailable.
  • Fixed: an exception from the AI Client could leave the report lock set. AI reports now request structured JSON output when the provider supports it.
  • Fixed: rewriting wp-config.php reset its permissions to 0644 and was not atomic. Writes now keep the existing permissions and replace the file atomically where the filesystem allows it.
  • Changed: AI availability no longer counts as a security warning, and application passwords are only a warning when administrator accounts have them.
  • Changed: the Wordfence feed is downloaded only when installed plugins or themes change or the 12-hour cache expires; version updates are re-matched locally. Feed severity ratings are used when available.
  • Changed: the optional HSTS header no longer includes includeSubDomains by default (filter: lockora_hsts_header_value).
  • Changed: the client report footer can name your agency instead of the default credit.
  • Changed: only one scan runs at a time, and legacy pre-release constant names are no longer read (a notice names any that are still defined).

0.5.0

  • Added a privileged account audit that compares raw user capability records with normal WordPress Administrator queries.
  • Added detection and listing for hidden Administrators, direct capability grants, privileged custom roles, runtime-granted privileges, duplicate or malformed capability metadata, and multisite super administrators.
  • Added CSV, TXT, and clipboard exports for the privileged account inventory.

0.4.3

  • Tested with WordPress 7.1.
  • Fixed: an unreadable directory during the wp-content anomaly scan crashed the scan instead of reporting a warning, because the error path called a helper that does not exist.
  • Fixed: findings supplied through the lockora_vulnerability_findings filter are now validated before they are counted, scored, stored, or displayed, so a malformed entry from another plugin can no longer break a scan.
  • Fixed: core integrity and wp-content CSV exports no longer write a PHP 8.4 deprecation notice into the downloaded file.
  • Fixed: the temporary PHP execution probe is now removed from the uploads directory even when the loopback request times out, and stale probes are cleared at the start of every scan so they are no longer reported as executable uploads.
  • Added: vendor links in the plugin header, the plugin description, and the client report footer.

0.4.2

  • Refined finding cards with stronger visual hierarchy, compact file metrics, categorized path previews, and unified file action toolbars.

0.4.1

  • Added CSV and TXT exports plus clipboard copying for reported wp-content anomaly paths.

0.4.0

  • Added a bounded wp-content anomaly scan for executable uploads, unexpected executables outside standard code directories, runtime executables, and backup or secret-like files.
  • Added filters for wp-content allowlists, exclusions, executable and sensitive extensions, and scan/reporting limits.

0.3.2

  • Moved the Who Changed It? integration action from individual finding cards to a single action at the top of Findings.

0.3.1

  • Added CSV and TXT exports for WordPress core integrity results.
  • Added a clipboard action for unexpected WordPress core files.
  • Added guarded one-click rotation of authentication keys and salts stored directly in wp-config.php.

0.3.0

  • Added bounded scan history and current-versus-previous finding comparisons.
  • Added contextual links from findings to Who Changed It? or its WordPress.org listing.
  • Added the lockora_scan_completed action for scan-result integrations.

0.2.2

  • Added: style altered WordPress core files list items and heading in red color (#b32d2e) for enhanced visibility.

0.2.1

  • Fixed: core integrity checks now show the full list of altered/missing/extra files through an interactive collapsible UI details panel when there are more than 5 files.
  • Added: auto-trigger scan update when loading the admin dashboard after plugin upgrade, ensuring the detailed file lists are populated immediately without manual intervention.

0.2.0

  • Fixed: wp-config.php can now be found one directory above the WordPress root, matching core behavior.
  • Fixed: authentication salt checks now use runtime constants, so salts defined outside wp-config.php (for example Bedrock-style configs) are no longer reported as missing and can no longer receive duplicate defines.
  • Fixed: generated salts can no longer be corrupted by regex replacement characters, and wp-config.php writes are now verified and rolled back if the written file does not match.
  • Fixed: admin notices are stored server-side instead of being read from the URL, removing a notice spoofing vector.
  • Fixed: network-activated plugins are no longer reported as inactive on multisite.
  • Fixed: the inactive administrator check now uses recorded last-login times instead of short-lived session tokens, removing false positives.
  • Fixed: the security header check falls back to GET when a server rejects HEAD requests, and the default fallback theme now follows WP_DEFAULT_THEME.
  • Added: public exposure checks for debug.log, readme.html, uploads directory listing, PHP execution in uploads, and author enumeration.
  • Added: SSL certificate expiry, database table prefix, automatic update posture, and login protection plugin checks.
  • Added: Site Health integration with a scan summary and key configuration tests.
  • Added: WP-CLI commands wp lockora scan and wp lockora report with JSON output and a –strict flag for CI.
  • Added: uninstall cleanup that removes all plugin options, transients, and user meta on deletion.
  • Hardened: AI report generation now uses a lock against concurrent requests, sanitizes finding text before prompting, and instructs the model to treat finding text as untrusted data.

0.1.2

  • Lowered the required WordPress version to 6.0 for non-AI security scanning and hardening checks.
  • Kept AI client reports disabled unless WordPress 7.0+ AI Client support is available.

0.1.1

  • Fixed HTTP security header scanning when a server returns duplicate headers as arrays.

0.1.0

  • Initial prototype with manual scans, hardening checks, core integrity checks, PHP version checks, vulnerability posture checks, optional Wordfence feed matching, and optional client-ready AI reports.
